content: The results of the systematic review on household crowding and its association with various health outcomes are as follows: 1. Outcome 1a: Tuberculosis (TB) Among the 23 studies included for this outcome, at least half were of acceptable quality. Most studies addressed a clearly focused issue and accounted for important confounding factors in their analyses, with the exception of five studies (Gyawali 2012, Irfan 2017, Larcombe 2011, Pelissari 2017, and Tornee 2005). Additionally, the analysis of confounders was not clearly explained in Soburg 2011, Kapoor 2016, and Sacchi 2018, although the latter two were only available as abstracts. However, some studies, such as Larcombe 2011 and Soburg 2011, did not clearly report these domains. Only about one-fifth of the studies provided a clear explanation of how sample size was determined, while the rest either partially described or omitted this information. In at least 80% of the studies, it was unclear whether follow-up was complete or long enough. Overall, most studies provided adequate descriptions of statistical analyses and study participants, and their results were considered reliable and applicable to the local population. Studies of very high quality with low risk of bias included Corbett 2009, Harling and Castro 2013, Hill 2006, Lienhardt 2005, Khan 2016, and Tesema 2015. 2. Outcome 1b: Non-TB Infectious Diseases A total of 54 studies were included for this outcome. The majority were of very good quality based on risk of bias (RoB) assessments. Most studies addressed a clearly focused issue and were considered to have reliable results applicable to the local population. However, 10 studies were unclear about whether confounders were accounted for in the analysis. Twenty-five studies provided a description of how sample size was determined, while the remainder gave only partial or unclear information. Thirty-four studies adequately described statistical analyses, and 36 studies provided sufficient descriptions of study participants. However, information on whether follow-up was complete or long enough was often unclear. Studies with the lowest quality in terms of risk of bias included Auguet et al. 2016, Chattopadhyay et al. 2016, Mirabel et al. 2015, Sekhar et al. 2009, Phillips et al. 2014, and MacLennan et al. 2006. Conversely, studies such as Alvarado et al. 2016, Baillie et al. 2005, Brander et al. 2017, and others performed well across most domains. 3. Outcome 2: Gastroenteritis and Diarrheal Diseases Eleven cohort and case-control studies were included. All studies had at least one domain at high risk of bias, with the number of high-risk domains per study ranging from 1 to 5. The most common high-risk domains were the identification and consideration of confounders, reporting of sample size calculations, and descriptions of study participant characteristics. The most common unclear risk domains were related to whether follow-up was adequate or long enough. Two case-control studies had no domains at high risk of bias. 4. Outcomes 3 and 5: Mental Health, Including Stress Thirteen studies were included, most of which were of acceptable quality. All studies except Al-Hemiary 2015 and Cabieses 2012 described their statistical analyses, and all studies except Al-Hemiary 2015 accounted for confounders. Many of these studies were population-based surveys with likely sufficient sample sizes. Information on participation refusal rates and differences between responders and non-responders was generally lacking. Five studies were published more than five years after data collection, but these were secondary analyses of previously collected data, which justified the delay. 5. Outcome 4: Sleep Disorders Three studies were identified that examined the association between household crowding and sleep disorders. All three were of acceptable quality. Van der Spuy 2017 had very low risk of bias, while Johnson 2015 did not identify all relevant confounding factors and was unclear about the applicability of results to a local context. In summary, the systematic review provided a comprehensive assessment of the quality and findings of studies examining the relationship between household crowding and various health outcomes. The results were synthesized using GRADE evidence profile tables, which evaluated risk of bias, consistency, indirectness, and overall quality.
